misconceptions.label: Thinks only one direction counts
misconceptions.description: Believes the vertices must be named going one specific way round the shape (usually clockwise), and doubts or rejects a shape that is correctly named going the other way.

misconceptions.label: Expects the labels to start at A
misconceptions.description: Judges a shape's naming by whether the first vertex noticed is labelled A, instead of checking that the labels climb one at a time all the way around from wherever they happen to start.

misconceptions.label: Checks only part of the loop
misconceptions.description: Confirms a shape's naming from a couple of neighbouring vertices whose letters happen to climb correctly, and stops before tracing the rest of the way around.

misconceptions.label: Writes the letters in descending order
misconceptions.description: Traces the shape's vertices in the direction that makes the labels count down instead of climb, ending up with a clean run of consecutive letters in reverse order, without checking that the final order is actually ascending.

questions.stem: A pentagon has 5 vertices, each labelled with a different letter. Going around the shape clockwise, the labels are, in order: D, E, F, G, Q. A student checks the first four labels, sees that they climb the alphabet one letter at a time, and concludes that the pentagon is correctly named. Is the student right, and why?

canonical_solution.text_md: Check every consecutive pair of vertices going around the shape, not just the first few: D→E, E→F, F→G each climb one letter at a time.
The next edge, G→Q, is where the pattern already breaks: for the naming to hold, Q would have to be the very next letter after G, but it is not.

There is still one edge left in the cycle — the one that actually closes the loop back to the start, Q→D — but a single break is already enough to fail the naming, so that edge cannot rescue it. The pentagon is not correctly named as given, and checking only the first four labels, as the student did, would have missed the break entirely.

choices.text: Yes — the first four vertices climb one letter at a time, so the pentagon is correctly named.
No — the naming is wrong because the sequence does not start with the letter A.

No — the convention requires the letters to climb one at a time all the way around the shape and back to the start. After G the next vertex is Q, which does not continue the sequence, so the pentagon is not correctly named as given.
No — the labels must be read going anticlockwise instead, since a clockwise reading is never the correct convention.

questions.stem: A quadrilateral has 4 vertices, each labelled with a different letter. Going around the shape clockwise, starting from one particular vertex, the labels are, in order: J, G, H, I. Applying the convention that a figure's vertices are named in alphabetical order, what is the correct name for this quadrilateral?

canonical_solution.text_md: The four labels used are G, H, I and J — already consecutive letters of the alphabet.
The diagram happens to start listing them from J, partway around the shape, but the convention says to start naming from the alphabetically-first vertex, G, and keep going the same way around.
Reading clockwise from G, the vertices in order are G, H, I, J, so the correct name is GHIJ.

questions.stem: Points $C(3, 10)$ and $D(11, k)$ are such that $CD=\sqrt{289}$, where $k\geq0$. Find the value of $k$.

canonical_solution.text_md: Write down the distance formula and substitute: $CD=\sqrt{(x_{D}-x_{C})^{2}+(y_{D}-y_{C})^{2}}$, so $\sqrt{289}=\sqrt{(11-(3))^{2}+(k-(10))^{2}}$.
Take the square root of both sides: $k-(10)=\pm\sqrt{225}=\pm15$.

questions.stem: Point $P(-1, -4)$ and point $Q(x, 2)$ lie $10$ units apart. Find all possible values of $x$.

Substitute $A(3, 2)$ for $(x_{1}, y_{1})$ and $M(3, 0)$ for $M(x, y)$: $\begin{aligned}3&=\frac{3+x_{2}}{2}&0&=\frac{2+y_{2}}{2}\end{aligned}$

questions.stem: $EFGH$ is a parallelogram with vertices $E(1, 5)$, $F(-1, 4)$ and $G(6, -4)$. Find the coordinates of $H$ by using the fact that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.

canonical_solution.text_md: Since the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, the mid-point of $EG$ is equal to the mid-point of $FH$. First find the mid-point of $EG$, then use it together with $F$ to find the coordinates of $H$.
